claim: COVID-19 is a global pandemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus.
source: COVID-19 is a global pandemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Vabret et al., 2020 in the introduction.

claim: T cells play a key role in the adaptive antiviral immune response by killing infected cells and facilitating the selection of virus-specific antibodies.
source: T cells play a key role in the adaptive antiviral immune response by killing infected cells and facilitating the selection of virus-specific antibodies.
evidence: This is a general statement about T cell function supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell clones with transient clonal expansion after infection were identified in both donors.
source: In both donors, we identified CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell clones with transient clonal expansion after infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from longitudinal TCR sequencing presented in the manuscript.

claim: Characteristic motifs in TCR sequences of COVID-19-reactive clones show preferential occurrence in publicly available large dataset of repertoires from COVID-19 patients.
source: We describe characteristic motifs in TCR sequences of COVID-19-reactive clones and show preferential occurrence of these motifs in publicly available large dataset of repertoires from COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis comparing motif frequencies between COVID-19 patients and controls.

claim: The majority of infection-reactive clonotypes acquire memory phenotypes in both donors.
source: We show that in both donors, the majority of infection-reactive clonotypes acquire memory phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from FACS-sorted memory subpopulations.

claim: Certain T-cell clones were detected in the memory fraction at the pre-infection time point, suggesting participation of pre-existing cross-reactive memory T cells in the immune response to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Certain T-cell clones were detected in the memory fraction at the pre-infection time point, suggesting participation of pre-existing cross-reactive memory T cells in the immune response to SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is supported by data showing responding clones present in pre-infection samples and is speculative regarding cross-reactivity.

claim: In SARS-1 survivors, antigen-specific memory T cells were detected up to 11 years after the initial infection, when viral-specific antibodies were undetectable.
source: In SARS-1 survivors, antigen-specific memory T cells were detected up to 11 years after the initial infection, when viral-specific antibodies were undetectable (Ng et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The T-cell response was shown to be critical for protection in SARS-1-infected mice.
source: The T-cell response was shown to be critical for protection in SARS-1-infected mice (Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia have been reported to recover from symptomatic COVID-19.
source: Patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a genetic disorder associated with lack of B cells, have been reported to recover from symptomatic COVID-19 (Quinti et al., 2020; Soresina et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published case reports.

claim: T cells are sufficient for viral clearance in some COVID-19 cases.
source: Patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia, a genetic disorder associated with lack of B cells, have been reported to recover from symptomatic COVID-19 (Quinti et al., 2020; Soresina et al., 2020), suggesting that in some cases, T cells are sufficient for viral clearance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that patients without B cells can recover from COVID-19.

claim: Activated CD8+HLA–DR+CD38+ T cells in a mild case of COVID-19 significantly expand following symptom onset, reaching their peak frequency of 12% of CD8+ T cells on day 9 after symptom onset, and contract thereafter.
source: Thevarajan et al. showed that activated CD8+HLA–DR+CD38+ T cells in a mild case of COVID-19 significantly expand following symptom onset, reaching their peak frequency of 12% of CD8+ T cells on day 9 after symptom onset, and contract thereafter (Thevarajan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The average time from infection to the onset of symptoms is 5 days.
source: Given the average time of 5 days from infection to the onset of symptoms (Bi et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The dynamics and magnitude of T-cell response to SARS-CoV-2 is similar to that observed after immunization with live vaccines.
source: the dynamics and magnitude of T-cell response to SARS-CoV-2 is similar to that observed after immunization with live vaccines (Miller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and comparison to published data on vaccine responses.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells were detected in COVID-19 survivors by activation following stimulation with SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells were detected in COVID-19 survivors by activation following stimulation with SARS-CoV-2 proteins (Ni et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells were detected in COVID-19 survivors by viral protein-derived peptide pools.
source: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells were detected in COVID-19 survivors by activation following stimulation with SARS-CoV-2 proteins (Ni et al., 2020) or by viral protein-derived peptide pools (Weiskopf et al., 2020; Braun et al., 2020; Snyder et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Meckiff et al., 2020; Bacher et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Some of the T cells activated by peptide stimulation were shown to have a memory phenotype.
source: Some of the T cells activated by peptide stimulation were shown to have a memory phenotype (Weiskopf et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Mateus et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Some potentially cross-reactive CD4+ T cells were found in healthy donors.
source: some potentially cross-reactive CD4+ T cells were found in healthy donors (Braun et al., 2020; Grifoni et al., 2020; Sekine et al., 2020; Bacher et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: T cells recognise short pathogen-derived peptides presented on the cell surface of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) using hypervariable T-cell receptors (TCR).
source: T cells recognise short pathogen-derived peptides presented on the cell surface of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) using hypervariable T-cell receptors (TCR).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about T cell recognition.

claim: TCR repertoire sequencing allows for the quantitative tracking of T-cell clones in time, as they go through the expansion and contraction phases of the response.
source: TCR repertoire sequencing allows for the quantitative tracking of T-cell clones in time, as they go through the expansion and contraction phases of the response.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of TCR sequencing technology, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Quantitative longitudinal TCR sequencing is able to identify antigen-specific expanding and contracting T cells in response to yellow fever vaccination with high sensitivity and specificity.
source: It was previously shown that quantitative longitudinal TCR sequencing is able to identify antigen-specific expanding and contracting T cells in response to yellow fever vaccination with high sensitivity and specificity (Minervina et al., 2020; Pogorelyy et al., 2018; DeWitt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Clonal expansion and significant contraction from the peak of the response are distinctive traits of T-cell clones specific to the virus.
source: Not only clonal expansion but also significant contraction from the peak of the response are distinctive traits of T-cell clones specific to the virus (Pogorelyy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Donor W is female and donor M is male, both healthy young adults.
source: donor W female and donor M male (both healthy young adults)
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Both donors returned to their home country from one of the centres of the COVID-19 outbreak in Europe in the middle of March.
source: In the middle of March (day 0), donor W female and donor M male (both healthy young adults) returned to their home country from the one of the centres of the COVID-19 outbreak in Europe at the time.
evidence: This is a description of the study timeline and participant exposure.

claim: Both donors were put into strict self-quarantine for 14 days upon arrival.
source: Upon arrival, according to local regulations, they were put into strict self-quarantine for 14 days.
evidence: This is a description of the study protocol.

claim: On day 3 of self-isolation, both donors developed low-grade fever, fatigue, and myalgia, which lasted 4 days.
source: On day 3 of self-isolation, both developed low-grade fever, fatigue, and myalgia, which lasted 4 days
evidence: This is a description of clinical symptoms observed in the study participants.

claim: Donor M experienced a temporary loss of smell following the initial symptoms.
source: and was followed by a temporary loss of smell for donor M.
evidence: This is a description of clinical symptoms observed in donor M.

claim: Peripheral blood samples were collected from both donors on days 15, 30, 37, 45, and 85.
source: On days 15, 30, 37, 45, and 85, we collected peripheral blood samples from both donors (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sampling schedule, also shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The presence of IgG and IgM SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies in the plasma was measured at all time points using SARS-CoV-2 S-RBD domain-specific ELISA.
source: The presence of IgG and IgM SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies in the plasma was measured at all time points using SARS-CoV-2 S-RBD domain-specific ELISA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to measure antibodies, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PBMCs, CD4+, and CD8+ T cells were isolated from each blood sample.
source: From each blood sample, we isolated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs, in two biological replicates), CD4+, and CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental cell isolation procedure.

claim: Four T-cell memory subpopulations (EM, EMRA, CM, and SCM) were isolated on days 30, 45, and 85.
source: Additionally, on days 30, 45, and 85, we isolated four T-cell memory subpopulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a): effector memory (EM: CCR7−CD45RA−), effector memory with CD45RA re-expression (EMRA: CCR7−CD45RA+), central memory (CM: CCR7+CD45RA−), and stem cell-like memory (SCM: CCR7+CD45RA+CD95+).
evidence: This describes the experimental isolation of memory subpopulations, with gating strategy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: TCRalpha and TCRbeta repertoire sequencing was performed on all samples.
source: From all samples, we isolated RNA and performed TCRalpha and TCRbeta repertoire sequencing as previously described (Pogorelyy et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental sequencing procedure.

claim: TCRalpha and TCRbeta repertoires were obtained for both donors 1 and 2 years prior to infection.
source: For both donors, TCRalpha and TCRbeta repertoires were obtained for other projects 1 and 2 years prior to infection.
evidence: This describes the availability of pre-infection data.

claim: TCR repertoires of multiple samples for donor M, including sorted memory subpopulations, are available from a published longitudinal TCR sequencing study after yellow fever vaccination.
source: Additionally, TCR repertoires of multiple samples for donor M – including sorted memory subpopulations – are available from a published longitudinal TCR sequencing study after yellow fever vaccination (donor M1 samples in Minervina et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the availability of additional data from a previous study.

claim: Principal component analysis of clonal temporal trajectories identifies three groups of clones with distinctive behaviours in both donors.
source: In both donors, and in both TCRalpha and TCRbeta repertoires, we identified three clusters of clones with distinct dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1b,c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b.

claim: The first cluster of clones had constant concentrations across time points.
source: The first cluster (Figure 1b,c, purple) corresponded to abundant TCR clonotypes that had constant concentrations across time points
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis and trajectory plots shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: The second cluster of clones showed contraction dynamics from day 15 to day 85.
source: the second cluster (Figure 1b,c, green) showed contraction dynamics from day 15 to day 85
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis and trajectory plots shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: The third cluster of clones showed clonal expansion from day 15 with a peak on day 37 followed by contraction.
source: and the third cluster (Figure 1b,c, yellow) showed an unexpected clonal expansion from day 15 with a peak on day 37 followed by contraction.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis and trajectory plots shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: The clustering and dynamics are similar in both donors and are reproduced in TCRbeta and TCRalpha repertoires.
source: The clustering and dynamics are similar in both donors and are reproduced in TCRbeta (Figure 1b,c) and TCRalpha (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b) repertoires.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of results across donors and TCR chains shown in multiple figures.

claim: 291 TCRalpha and 295 TCRbeta clonotypes in donor W and 607 TCRalpha and 616 TCRbeta in donor M were significantly contracted from day 15 to day 85.
source: We identified 291 TCRalpha and 295 TCRbeta clonotypes in donor W and 607 TCRalpha and 616 TCRbeta in donor M significantly contracted from day 15 to day 85
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis using edgeR and NoisET methods.

claim: 176 TCRalpha and 278 TCRbeta for donor W and 293 TCRalpha and 427 TCRbeta clonotypes for donor M were significantly expanded from days 15 to 37.
source: One hundred and seventy six TCRalpha and 278 TCRbeta for donor W and 293 TCRalpha and 427 TCRbeta clonotypes for donor M were significantly expanded from days 15 to 37
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis using edgeR and NoisET methods.

claim: Contracting clones corresponded to 2.5% and 0.9% of T cells on day 15 post-infection for donors M and W, respectively.
source: Contracting clones corresponded to 2.5% and 0.9% of T cells on day 15 post-infection, expanding clones reached 1.1% and 0.8% on day 37 for donors M and W, respectively (Figure 1d,e, left).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of clonotype frequencies shown in Figure 1d,e.

claim: Expanding clones reached 1.1% and 0.8% of T cells on day 37 for donors M and W, respectively.
source: Contracting clones corresponded to 2.5% and 0.9% of T cells on day 15 post-infection, expanding clones reached 1.1% and 0.8% on day 37 for donors M and W, respectively (Figure 1d,e, left).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of clonotype frequencies shown in Figure 1d,e.

claim: The magnitude of the T-cell response to COVID-19 is of the same order of magnitude as previously observed after live yellow fever vaccine immunization of donor M (6.7% T cells on day 15 post-vaccination).
source: This magnitude of the T-cell response is of the same order of magnitude as previously observed after live yellow fever vaccine immunization of donor M (6.7% T cells on day 15 post-vaccination).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published data from the same donor.

claim: Both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets participated actively in the response.
source: Both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets participated actively in the response (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by phenotyping data shown in Figure 1d,e.

claim: A recent study reported activation of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells in COVID-19 patients.
source: A recent study by Parrot et al., 2020 reported activation of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: MAIT cells are innate-like T cells recognising bacterial metabolites with TCRs featuring an invariant TCRalpha chain.
source: MAIT cells are innate-like T cells recognising bacterial metabolites with TCRs featuring an invariant TCRalpha chain.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about MAIT cells.

claim: A small number of low-frequency contracting and expanding TCRalpha clonotypes have MAIT invariant alpha chains.
source: We found that a small number of low-frequency contracting (one clonotype for each donor) and expanding (two clonotypes for each donor) TCRalpha clonotypes have MAIT invariant alpha chains
evidence: This is supported by comparison to a database of MAIT TCR sequences.

claim: The contribution of MAIT clonotypes to the response was relatively small (<1% of responding T cells are MAIT).
source: and the contribution of these clonotypes to the response was relatively small (<1% of responding T cells are MAIT).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of MAIT clonotype frequencies.

claim: Both contracting and expanding T-cell clones were found in memory subpopulations on days 30, 45, and 85.
source: On days 30, 45, and 85, we identified both contracting (Figure 2a–c) and expanding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c) T-cell clones in the memory subpopulations of peripheral blood.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of FACS-sorted memory subpopulations shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: Both CD4+ and CD8+ responding clones were found in the CM and EM subsets.
source: Both CD4+ and CD8+ responding clones were found in the CM and EM subsets
evidence: This is supported by analysis of memory subpopulation repertoires.

claim: CD4+ responding clones were more biased towards CM.
source: however, CD4+ were more biased towards CM (with exception of donor W day 30 time point, where a considerable fraction of CD8+ clones were found in CM)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of memory subpopulation distributions shown in Figure 2.

claim: CD8+ responding clones were more represented in the EMRA subset.
source: and CD8+ clones more represented in the EMRA subset.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of memory subpopulation distributions shown in Figure 2.

claim: A small number of both CD4+ and CD8+ responding clonotypes were identified in the SCM subpopulation.
source: A small number of both CD4+ and CD8+ responding clonotypes were also identified in the SCM subpopulation
evidence: This is supported by analysis of memory subpopulation repertoires.

claim: SCM is a long-lived T-cell memory subset.
source: which was previously shown to be a long-lived T-cell memory subset (Fuertes Marraco et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: A number of responding CD4+ clones, and fewer CD8+ clones, were represented in the repertoires of both donors 1 and 2 years before the infection.
source: Intriguingly, a number of responding CD4+ clones, and fewer CD8+ clones, were also represented in the repertoires of both donors 1 and 2 years before the infection.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pre-infection repertoire data.

claim: The majority of pre-existing clones had low concentrations at pre-infection and day 85 post-infection time points, and high concentrations on day 15.
source: The majority of the pre-existing clones had low concentrations at pre-infection and day 85 post-infection time points, and high concentrations on day 15, suggesting that they expanded after the infection and later contracted for both donors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal tracking of pre-existing clones shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pre-existing SARS-CoV-2-reactive CD4+ clones were identified in the CM subpopulation 1 year before the infection in donor M.
source: For donor M, for whom we had previously sequenced memory subpopulations before the infection (Minervina et al., 2020), we were able to identify pre-existing SARS-CoV-2-reactive CD4+ clones in the CM subpopulation 1 year before the infection
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pre-infection memory subpopulation data for donor M.

claim: A group of CD8+ clones were found in the pre-infection EM subpopulation in donor M.
source: and a group of CD8+ clones in the pre-infection EM subpopulation.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pre-infection memory subpopulation data for donor M.

claim: On day 30 after infection, the majority of pre-infection CM clones were detected in the EM subpopulation.
source: Interestingly, on day 30 after infection, the majority of pre-infection CM clones were detected in the EM subpopulation, suggesting recent T-cell activation and a switch of the phenotype from memory to effector.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of memory subpopulation distributions over time.

claim: Pre-existing clones might represent memory T cells cross-reactive for other infections, for example other human coronaviruses.
source: These clones might represent memory T cells cross-reactive for other infections, for example other human coronaviruses.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation of pre-existing responding clones.

claim: A search for TCRbeta amino acid sequences of responding clones in VDJdb resulted in essentially no overlap with TCRs not specific for SARS-CoV-2 epitopes.
source: A search for TCRbeta amino acid sequences of responding clones in VDJdb (Bagaev et al., 2020) — a database of TCRs with known specificities — resulted in essentially no overlap with TCRs not specific for SARS-CoV-2 epitopes: only two clonotypes matched.
evidence: This is supported by database search results.

claim: One VDJdb match corresponded to a cytomegalovirus epitope presented by the HLA-A*03 MHC allele, which is absent in both donors.
source: One match corresponded to the cytomegalovirus epitope presented by the HLA-A*03 MHC allele, which is absent in both donors (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is supported by database search and HLA typing data.

claim: One VDJdb match was for an Influenza A virus epitope presented by HLA-A*02 allele.
source: and a second match was for Influenza A virus epitope presented by HLA-A*02 allele.
evidence: This is supported by database search results.

claim: The absence of VDJdb matches suggests that contracting and expanding clones are unlikely to be specific for immunodominant epitopes of common pathogens covered in VDJdb.
source: The absence of matches suggests that contracting and expanding clones are unlikely to be specific for immunodominant epitopes of common pathogens covered in VDJdb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of database matches.

claim: On day 25 post-infection, donor M's CD8+ T cells were stained with a HLA-A*02:01-YLQPRTFLL MHC-I tetramer.
source: On day 25, post-infection donor M participated in a study by Shomuradova et al., 2020 (as donor p1434), where his CD8+ T cells were stained with a HLA-A*02:01-YLQPRTFLL MHC-I tetramer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This describes an independent validation experiment from another study.

claim: TCRalpha and TCRbeta of FACS-sorted tetramer-positive cells were sequenced and deposited to VDJdb.
source: TCRalpha and TCRbeta of FACS-sorted tetramer-positive cells were sequenced and deposited to VDJdb (see Shomuradova et al., 2020 for the experimental details).
evidence: This describes the availability of validation data from another study.

claim: All matching tetramer-positive clonotypes had a CD8+ phenotype.
source: (as expected for TCRs specifically binding MHC-I multimer, all matching clonotypes in our datasets had a CD8+ phenotype).
evidence: This is supported by phenotyping data and is consistent with MHC-I restriction.

claim: No tetramer-positive clonotypes matched with expanding clonotypes peaking on day 37.
source: No tetramer-positive clonotypes matched with expanding clonotypes peaking on day 37.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of tetramer-positive TCRs to expanding clones.

claim: TCRs recognising the same antigens frequently have highly similar TCR sequences.
source: It was previously shown that TCRs recognising the same antigens frequently have highly similar TCR sequences (Dash et al., 2017; Glanville et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The number of edges in all similarity networks except CD8+ expanding clones was significantly larger than would be expected by randomly sampling the same number of clonotypes from the corresponding repertoire.
source: The number of edges in all similarity networks except CD8+ expanding clones was significantly larger than would expected by randomly sampling the same number of clonotypes from the corresponding repertoire (Figure 3d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison to random samples shown in the figures.

claim: Clusters of highly similar clones were found in both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets for expanding and contracting clonotypes in both donors.
source: In both donors, we found clusters of highly similar clones in both CD4+ and CD8+ subsets for expanding and contracting clonotypes.
evidence: This is supported by similarity network analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Clusters were largely donor specific.
source: Clusters were largely donor specific, as expected, since our donors have dissimilar HLA alleles (Supplementary file 2) and thus each is likely to present a non-overlapping set of T-cell antigens.
evidence: This is an inference based on HLA typing data and knowledge of MHC restriction.

claim: The largest cluster was described by the motif TRAV35-CAGXNYGGSQGNLIF-TRAJ42 and was identified in donor M's CD4+-contracting alpha chains.
source: The largest cluster, described by the motif TRAV35-CAGXNYGGSQGNLIF-TRAJ42, was identified in donor M's CD4+-contracting alpha chains.
evidence: This is supported by sequence motif analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Clones from the largest cluster constituted 16.3% of all of donor M's CD4+-responding cells on day 15.
source: Clones from this cluster constituted 16.3% of all of donor M's CD4+-responding cells on day 15, suggesting a response to an immunodominant CD4+ epitope in the SARS-CoV-2 proteome.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of cluster frequencies.

claim: The high similarity of TCR sequences in the largest cluster allowed independent identification of motifs using the ALICE algorithm.
source: The high similarity of the TCR sequences of responding clones in this cluster allowed us to independently identify motifs from donor M's CD4 alpha contracting clones using the ALICE algorithm (Pogorelyy et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ALICE analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 32 CD8+ TCRbetas were mapped to SARS-CoV-2 peptides using the MIRA dataset.
source: This procedure yielded unambiguous matches for 32 CD8+ TCRbetas – just one clonotype was paired to two peptide pools (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by matching analysis to the MIRA database.

claim: The vast majority of matches to MIRA corresponded to groups of contracting clones.
source: The vast majority of matches to MIRA corresponded to groups of contracting clones.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of MIRA matches to contracting/expanding clone sets.

claim: All clusters corresponding to HLA-A*02:01-YLQPRTFLL MHC-I tetramer-specific TCRs were matched to the peptide pool YLQPRTFL,YLQPRTFLL,YYVGYLQPRTF in the MIRA dataset.
source: As expected, we found that all clusters corresponding to HLA-A*02:01-YLQPRTFLL MHC-I tetramer-specific TCRs were matched to the peptide pool YLQPRTFL,YLQPRTFLL,YYVGYLQPRTF in the MIRA dataset.
evidence: This validates the MIRA mapping approach using tetramer data.

claim: Another large group of matches corresponded to the HLA-B*15:01-restricted NQKLIANQF epitope.
source: Another large group of matches corresponded to the HLA-B*15:01-restricted (Stamatakis et al., 2020) NQKLIANQF epitope.
evidence: This is supported by MIRA mapping and citation to a study identifying the HLA restriction.

claim: Clonotypes corresponding to the NQKLIANQF cluster together made up 21% of the CD8+ immune response on day 15.
source: Interestingly, clonotypes corresponging to this cluster together made up 21% of the CD8+ immune response on day 15, suggesting immunodominance of this epitope.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of cluster frequencies shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Two TCRbeta clonotypes mapped to the NQKLIANQF epitope were identified in Effector Memory subset 1 year before the infection.
source: Two TCRbeta clonotypes mapped to this epitope were identified in Effector Memory subset 1 year before the infection, suggesting potential cross-reactive response.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pre-infection memory subpopulation data.

claim: The NQKLIANQF response might be initially triggered by NQKLIANAF, a homologous HLA-B*15:01 epitope from HKU1 or OC43 common human betacoronaviruses.
source: We speculate that this response might be initially triggered by NQKLIANAF, a homologous HLA-B*15:01 epitope from HKU1 or OC43, common human betacoronaviruses.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the origin of cross-reactive T cells.

claim: No matches for the NQKLIANQF epitope were observed among contracting or expanding clonotypes of HLA-B*15-negative donor W.
source: Importantly, no matches for the NQKLIANQF epitope were observed among contracting or expanding clonotypes of HLA-B*15-negative donor W (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of MIRA matches between donors with different HLA types.

claim: Consistent pairing was found between one of the motifs in TCRalpha to the largest motif in TCRbeta T cells associated with HLA-B*15:01-NQKLIANQF.
source: We found consistent pairing between one of the motifs in TCRalpha to the largest motif in TCRbeta T cells, which is associated with HLA-B*15:01-NQKLIANQF.
evidence: This is supported by computational alpha/beta pairing analysis.

claim: The total frequency of TCRbeta sequences forming the largest cluster in donor M is significantly larger in the COVID-19 cohort than in the healthy donor cohort.
source: In Figure 4c,d, we show that the total frequency of TCRbeta sequences forming the largest cluster in donor M (Figure 4c) and donor W (Figure 4d) is significantly larger in the COVID-19 cohort than in the healthy donor cohort from Emerson et al., 2017, suggesting antigen-dependent clonal expansion.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of motif frequencies between COVID-19 and control cohorts shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: The total frequency of TCRbeta sequences forming the largest cluster in donor W is significantly larger in the COVID-19 cohort than in the healthy donor cohort.
source: In Figure 4c,d, we show that the total frequency of TCRbeta sequences forming the largest cluster in donor M (Figure 4c) and donor W (Figure 4d) is significantly larger in the COVID-19 cohort than in the healthy donor cohort from Emerson et al., 2017, suggesting antigen-dependent clonal expansion.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of motif frequencies between COVID-19 and control cohorts shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: The CD4+ TCRbeta motif from donor W occurs preferentially in donors predicted to have DRB1*07:01 allele.
source: We found that the CD4+ TCRbeta motif from donor W occurs preferentially in donors predicted to have DRB1*07:01 allele
evidence: This is supported by HLA prediction analysis and motif frequency comparison.

claim: The CD4+ TCRbeta motif from donor M appears to be associated with HLA-DRB1*03:01-DQB1*02:01 haplotype.
source: while the motif from donor M appears to be associated with HLA-DRB1*03:01-DQB1*02:01 haplotype.
evidence: This is supported by HLA prediction analysis and motif frequency comparison.

claim: The frequency of sequences corresponding to CD4+ motifs can be used to identify SARS-CoV-2 infected donors with matching HLA alleles.
source: The frequency of sequences corresponding to these motifs can then be used to identify SARS-CoV-2 infected donors with matching HLA alleles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A group of predominantly CD4+ clonotypes expanded from day 15 to day 37 after the infection in both donors.
source: Surprisingly, in both donors, we also identified a group of predominantly CD4+ clonotypes that expanded from day 15 to day 37 after the infection.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and PCA of clonal trajectories.

claim: One possible explanation for the second wave of expansion is the priming of CD4+ T cells by antigen-specific B cells.
source: One possible explanation for this second wave of expansion is the priming of CD4+ T cells by antigen-specific B cells, but there might be other mechanisms such as the migration of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells from lymphoid organs or bystander activation of non-SARS-CoV-2 specific T cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed expanding clone dynamics.

claim: Later expanding T cells might be triggered by another infection, simultaneously and asymptomatically occurring in both donors around day 30.
source: It is also possible that later expanding T cells are triggered by another infection, simultaneously and asymptomatically occurring in both donors around day 30.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation for the expanding clone dynamics.

claim: A large fraction of putatively SARS-CoV-2-reactive T cell clones are found in memory subpopulations and remain there at least 3 months after infection.
source: We showed that a large fraction of putatively SARS-CoV-2-reactive T cell clones are later found in memory subpopulations and remain there at least 3 months after infection.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of memory subpopulation repertoires at multiple time points.

claim: Some responding clones are found in long-lived stem cell-like memory (SCM) subset.
source: Importantly, some of responding clones are found in long-lived stem cell-like memory (SCM) subset, as also reported for SARS-CoV-2 convalescent patients in Sekine et al., 2020.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SCM repertoires and citation to another study with similar findings.

claim: A subset of CD4+ clones were identified in pre-infection central memory subsets.
source: A subset of CD4+ clones were identified in pre-infection central memory subsets, and a subset of CD8+ T cells were found in effector memory.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pre-infection memory subpopulation data.

claim: A subset of CD8+ T cells were found in pre-infection effector memory.
source: A subset of CD4+ clones were identified in pre-infection central memory subsets, and a subset of CD8+ T cells were found in effector memory.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of pre-infection memory subpopulation data.

claim: Pre-existing CD8+ clones recognising NQKLIANQF include an immunodominant HLA-B*15:01 restricted SARS-CoV-2 epitope for which a homologous epitope differing by 1 aa mismatch exists in common human betacoronaviruses.
source: Among these are CD8+ clones recognising NQKLIANQF, an immunodominant HLA-B*15:01 restricted SARS-CoV-2 epitope, for which homologous epitope differing by 1 aa mismatch exists in common human betacoronaviruses.
evidence: This is supported by epitope mapping and sequence comparison to other coronavirus epitopes.

claim: The presence of SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD4+ T cells in healthy individuals was recently demonstrated.
source: The presence of SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD4+ T cells in healthy individuals was recently demonstrated (Braun et al., 2020; Grifoni et al., 2020; Le Bert et al., 2020; Meckiff et al., 2020; Bacher et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Cross-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells can participate in the response in vivo.
source: Our data further suggests that cross-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells can participate in the response in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of pre-existing responding clones.

claim: Larger studies with cohorts of severe and mild cases with pre-infection time points are needed to determine whether the presence of cross-reactive T cells before infection is linked to the mildness of the disease.
source: It is interesting to ask whether the presence of cross-reactive T cells before infection is linked to the mildness of the disease (with predicted HLA-B*15:01 cross-reactive epitope described above as a good starting point). Larger studies with cohorts of severe and mild cases with pre-infection time points are needed to address this question.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions and limitations of the current study.
